prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You ever wake up with your footie PJs warming your neck like a noose? Ever upchuck after a home-cooked meal? Or notice how the blood on the bottoms of your feet just won’t seem to go away? Love, it used to be you could retire your toothbrush for like two or three days and still I’d push my downy face into your neck. Used to be I hung on your every word. (Sing! you’d say: and I was a bird.Freedom! you’d say: and I never really knew what that meant, but liked the way it rang like a rusty bell.) Used to be. But now I can tell you your breath stinks and you’re full of shit. You have more lies about yourself than bodies beneath your bed. Rootingfor the underdog. Team player. Hook, line and sinker. Love, you helped design the brick that built the walls around the castle in the basement of which is a vault inside of which is another vault inside of which . . . you get my point. Your tongue is made of honey but flicks like a snake’s. Voice like a bird but everyone’s ears are bleeding. From the inside your house shines and shines, but from outside you can see it’s built from bones. From out here it looks like a graveyard, and the garden’s all ash. And besides, your breath stinks. We’re through.

The speaker confronts a former beloved’s hypocrisy, lies, and moral corruption through a direct breakup address filled with grotesque imagery and sharp metaphors. The result is a complete rejection of the beloved’s false charm, revealing that what once seemed beautiful is actually rotten, oppressive, and built on harm.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, PJs, Ever

outputs.L1:
Have you ever woken to find your footie pajamas warming your neck like a noose? Have you ever vomited after a home-cooked meal? Or noticed how the blood on the bottoms of your feet simply will not seem to go away?

Love, there was a time when you could retire your toothbrush for two or three days, and still I would press my downy face into your neck. There was a time when I hung on your every word. “Sing!” you would say, and I was a bird. “Freedom!” you would say, and though I never truly knew what that meant, I liked the way it rang like a rusty bell.

There was a time.

But now I can tell you that your breath stinks and you are full of shit. You have more lies about yourself than bodies beneath your bed: rooting for the underdog; team player; hook, line, and sinker.

Love, you helped design the brick that built the walls around the castle, in the basement of which is a vault, inside of which is another vault, inside of which . . . you get my point.

Your tongue is made of honey, but it flicks like a snake’s. Your voice is like a bird’s, but everyone’s ears are bleeding. From the inside, your house shines and shines; but from the outside, one can see it is built from bones. From out here, it looks like a graveyard, and the garden is all ash.

And besides, your breath stinks.

We are through.
outputs.L2:
Have you ever come to consciousness with the collar of your footed pajamas cinched hot around your throat, almost like a rope? Have you ever vomited after eating something made at home? Have you ever realized the blood staining the soles of your feet simply refuses to wash off?

Darling, there was a time when you could abandon your toothbrush for two, maybe three days, and I would still bury my soft, feathered face against your neck. Back then, I listened as if every syllable you spoke mattered. “Sing!” you would command, and I became a bird. “Freedom!” you would cry, and though I never truly understood the word, I loved its clang, like an old corroded bell.

That was then.

Now I can say plainly that your breath is foul and you’re made of lies. You’ve invented more false stories about who you are than there are corpses hidden under your bed. Champion of the little guy. Good teammate. Swallowed it all without question. Sweetheart, you had a hand in making the very brick used to raise the walls around the castle, and beneath that castle sits a vault, and inside that vault is another vault, and inside that—well, you understand.

Your words drip sweetness, but your tongue strikes like a serpent. Your voice may sound birdlike, yet everyone who hears it is bleeding from the ears. Inside, your house gleams and gleams; from the outside, though, anyone can see it was assembled from bones. From where I stand, it resembles a cemetery, and the garden has turned entirely to ash.

Also, your breath reeks.

It’s over between us.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses a former lover in a tone of bitter disillusionment and disgust. What may once have been affection has curdled into anger, contempt, and emotional exhaustion. The relationship is presented not as something sadly lost, but as something the speaker now recognizes as corrupt and damaging.

A strong contrast is established between the speaker’s past devotion and their present clarity. In the past, the speaker may have been blinded by love, charm, or desire, unable—or unwilling—to see the lover’s true nature. Now, however, that illusion has been shattered. The speaker can see the lover’s flaws plainly and no longer excuses or romanticizes their behavior.

The former lover is portrayed as deceptive and hypocritical, someone who hides selfish motives behind attractive words or gestures. Their lies are not presented as harmless mistakes, but as self-serving manipulations. The speaker suggests that the lover’s identity has been built on falsehood: they pretend to be loving, sincere, or admirable, while in reality they are dishonest and morally empty.

The imagery surrounding the lover reinforces this sense of betrayal. Any beauty, charm, or outward appeal they possess is shown to conceal something much darker. Beneath the surface lies violence, decay, and moral corruption. This contrast between appearance and reality makes the lover seem not merely flawed, but dangerous and repulsive. Their attractiveness becomes a mask hiding ugliness underneath.

By the end, the speaker takes decisive control of the situation. The declaration “We’re through” marks a final break from the relationship and from the illusions that sustained it. It is not a hesitant or regretful farewell, but a firm rejection. The speaker refuses to remain trapped by deception any longer and ends the relationship with certainty and finality.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses a former beloved directly, turning what might have been a tender farewell into a fierce act of accusation and rejection. Rather than mourning the end of love, the speaker exposes the beloved’s hypocrisy, dishonesty, and moral decay. The beloved may once have appeared charming, beautiful, or worthy of devotion, but that surface attractiveness is now revealed as a disguise. Through harsh, grotesque imagery and cutting metaphors, the speaker strips away the illusion of innocence and shows the beloved as corrupt beneath the surface.

The breakup is therefore not simply emotional but moral. The speaker condemns the beloved’s lies, cruelty, and false virtue, suggesting that their beauty has always been connected to harm. What once seemed sweet or desirable is described as rotten, oppressive, and poisonous. The beloved’s charm is no longer enchanting; it is exposed as a trap, a mask that conceals selfishness and damage. By using violent and disturbing images, the speaker makes clear that the relationship was not merely disappointing but destructive.

In the end, the poem or speech becomes a complete rejection of the beloved and everything they represent. The speaker refuses to be deceived any longer by appearances, false affection, or seductive language. Love is replaced by disgust, and admiration gives way to judgment. The former beloved is no longer seen as beautiful, but as morally diseased and complicit in suffering. The speaker’s final stance is one of liberation: by naming the beloved’s corruption, they free themselves from the illusion that once held power over them.
outputs.L5:
You slip into your favorite PJs at the end of a long day, and suddenly the world feels a little softer. The lights dim, the room grows quiet, and everything that seemed urgent begins to fade away. There is something comforting about those small evening rituals—the warm drink, the familiar blanket, the peaceful pause before sleep.

Ever notice how the simplest moments can feel the most meaningful? It is not always the big adventures or perfect plans that stay with us. Sometimes it is the calm of being exactly where you are, dressed in cozy PJs, letting yourself rest without guilt.

You deserve those moments. You deserve comfort, quiet, and the gentle reminder that tomorrow can wait.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, darkly comic breakup monologue addressed to “Love,” in a grotesque fairy-tale voice, full of bodily imagery, betrayal, and strange metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
Love, you damp little prince in a coat made of tongues,

I have come to return your gifts.

Here is the glass slipper, still full of my blood. Here is the singing apple with the bite taken out, still humming your name through its wormholes. Here is the ring you slipped onto my finger while I slept, which has since grown teeth and gnawed the knuckle down to a pearl.

Do not look at me with those wet cathedral eyes. I know your tricks. I know the way you arrive dressed as a rescue and leave as a landlord. You build a castle in the softest part of the body, hang curtains in the spleen, put your boots on the heart, and then complain about the drafts.

I was a fool, yes, a maiden with bread in her apron and bells in her hair, skipping toward your gingerbread house like a lamb with excellent manners. You opened the door in a crown of candlewax and said, Come in, my darling, there is soup. And because I was starving, because the world had been so full of wolves with polite moustaches, I sat at your table.

The soup was made of promises. Naturally, I drank the whole pot.

Then came the usual enchantments: the moon turning into a plate; the bed turning into a boat; my ribs opening like cupboard doors to let you rummage among the china. You praised my little organs. “How brave,” you said, pinching my liver. “How loyal,” you said, braiding my intestines into a bridal veil.

And I blushed! Imagine it. Me, sitting there with my lungs fluttering like two poisoned doves, grateful to be rearranged.

But Love, you are a butcher with lullabies.

You said forever, and meant until breakfast. You said beloved, and meant convenient animal. You said trust me, and out came the sack, the river, the millstone, the old familiar splash.

Do you remember the night you fed my secrets to the swans? They circled the pond afterward with my childhoods hanging from their beaks, honking like aristocrats. Do you remember how you kissed my forehead with your mouth full of someone else’s name? It fell between us on the pillow, slick and newborn, and began to cry.

I tried to forgive it. I swaddled the name. I rocked it. I told myself all babies are ugly at first.

But it grew.

Soon it was crawling through the pantry, eating the jam, wearing my shoes, calling you Papa.

Oh, Love. You cheating little goblin. You velvet infection. You banquet where every course is my own face served back to me with parsley.

I should have known when the birds stopped singing and began taking notes. I should have known when the mirror, that silver gossip, spat whenever I asked if I was still fair. I should have known when your shadow detached itself and started courting mine behind the wardrobe.

But no. I polished your lies until I could see my reflection in them. I slept beside you while the mattress filled with eels. I called it devotion when you handed me the knife and said, Cut away everything that does not please me.

So I did.

First went my anger, a red hen flapping in the yard. Then my appetite, poor piglet, squealing. Then my pride, that tall black horse, led gently into the forest and never seen again. By the end I was so dainty, so hollow, I could be lifted by a rumor.

And still you sighed and said I was too much.

Too much! Me, with my heart folded into a napkin. Me, with my tongue trained to sit, stay, roll over. Me, who made myself small enough to live inside the dimple in your left cheek, paying rent in apologies.

Well.

The spell is broken. The pumpkin has rotted. The mice have unionized. The fairy godmother is drunk in a ditch, waving her wand at passing carts and turning them into tax problems.

And I am leaving.

Do not send the huntsman. I ate him.

Do not send the seven dwarfs. I have no patience for small men with pickaxes.

Do not climb my hair. I have cut it off and used it to floss your vows from between my teeth.

I am taking back my name from your mouth. You have stretched it out, chewed it, taught it to beg. I will wash it in nettles. I will hang it on a thorn bush to dry. By morning it will fit me again.

I am taking back my body, too. Every haunted room of it. The attic where you stored your weather. The cellar where your excuses grew fur. The kitchen where my hope sat in a pot, boiling down to glue. I evict you from the wrists, the throat, the soft under-knee. I evict you from the scar shaped like a question mark. I evict you from the belly, where you built a chapel and charged admission.

Out, Love. Out with your lace cuffs and your plague cart. Out with your bouquet of fingers. Out with the tiny orchestra that plays whenever I remember being touched kindly.

I will miss nothing except the fever, and perhaps the fever’s little hat.

Tomorrow I will wake in my own bed, which is not a boat, not an altar, not a grave with pillows. I will breakfast on black coffee and the last of your letters, toasted crisp. I will laugh, and the laugh will come out crooked, dragging chains, smelling faintly of grave soil—but it will be mine.

Then I will go into the woods.

Not to be rescued. Not to be kissed awake. Not to marry the first man who can identify my shoe.

I will go to meet the wolf.

He and I have always had more in common anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short prose poem where a once-devoted pet or familiar finally tells off its owner, mixing affection, horror, and accusations of hypocrisy.
counterfactuals.output:
You called me faithful when I warmed your feet, monstrous when I brought you what the night had given me. You kissed the soft place between my ears with a mouth that blessed mercy, then set traps for mice in the pantry and prayers for saints above the bed. Master, I loved you with my whole small furnace of a body. I learned the weather of your hands, forgave the boot, the locked door, the days you forgot my bowl and named it sorrow.

But do not ask me to purr at your innocence.

I have seen you bury worse things than bones. I have watched you wash blood from your cuffs and call it duty, watched you fear my yellow eyes because they remember. You made me your familiar, your little shadow, your velvet sin-eater; then shuddered when I spoke in the voice you poured into me.

So hear me now: I am not wicked for hunting. I am honest. I never pretended the moon was clean.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental flash fiction piece in second person that starts with bizarre questions about footie pajamas, vomit, and blood on feet, then spirals into a lyrical rejection.
counterfactuals.output:
Are you still wearing the footie pajamas with the moons chewed off the toes? Did you vomit in the hallway again, or was that someone else’s small green weather? Whose blood is on your feet, and why did you walk it into the kitchen like a red carpet for no one?

You don’t answer because answers are doors, and you have always preferred windows: exitless, bright, pretending at escape.

The house hums around you. The refrigerator rehearses its one-note opera. The pipes knock like a polite ghost asking to be remembered. Somewhere, a phone is ringing inside a drawer full of teeth, or maybe buttons, or maybe all the apologies you refused to alphabetize.

You think of love as a room you were told to enter quietly.

You entered quietly.

You think of yourself as a match struck underwater.

Still, you are here: damp flame, impossible witness, little catastrophe in fleece.

I could say come closer. I could say let me wash your feet. I could say the moon is a bowl and we are what spilled from it. But I have learned the grammar of your ruin: every tenderness becomes a leash if tied around the wrong throat.

So no.

No, I will not be the towel.  
No, I will not be the sink.  
No, I will not kneel in the bright little chapel of your mess and call it mercy.

You blink, and the wallpaper flowers open their mouths. They sing in the language of mildew. They sing your name the way hospitals do: surname first, soul last. You reach for me with hands that smell like pennies and sleep, hands that have held too many endings without washing.

But listen: even the dark has a spine.

Even the lake refuses the stone after swallowing it.

Even the dog at the edge of the highway turns away from the bone when the bone begins to speak.

I am turning away.

Not because I do not know you. Because I do. Because I know the soft trap of your need, the velvet pit, the lullaby with barbed wire braided through it. Because I have worn your sadness like a borrowed coat and found my own arms missing. Because every time you say stay, a bird falls silent in my chest.

You stand there, moonless, blood-footed, a child-costumed omen, and the hallway lengthens behind you into every winter we survived badly.

I place my refusal on the floor between us.

It is small at first. A seed. A tooth. A white button from a dead man’s shirt.

Then it grows antlers.

Then it grows wings.

Then it becomes a door made entirely of morning.

You say my name.

I let it pass through me.

A thread through smoke.

A hook through water.

A prayer addressed to an empty field.

No, I say, and the house exhales. No, I say, and the refrigerator stops singing. No, I say, and somewhere inside the walls, all the hidden teeth loosen from their gums.

You are still wearing the footie pajamas.

You are still standing in the red print of yourself.

But I am no longer the floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a caustic breakup letter in the style of contemporary literary horror: intimate, poetic, funny, and vicious, ending with “We’re through.”
counterfactuals.output:
Dear You,

I have been meaning to leave you for months, but I kept mistaking the scratching in the walls for weather. Then I realized it was my own self-respect, trapped between the studs, gnawing its way toward daylight.

You loved me the way mold loves bread: thoroughly, invisibly at first, then all at once so everyone could smell it. You moved through my life in damp socks, leaving little gray footprints on everything I cared about. My friends. My sleep. My ability to hear the word “honestly” without flinching.

I used to think you were complicated. You are not. You are a haunted house with no ghost, just bad plumbing and an owner who keeps insisting the screams are “character.” You call your cruelty “communication.” You call your laziness “healing.” You call every woman who has ever escaped you “crazy,” which is fascinating, considering you are a haunted doll with a podcast microphone.

I hope you find someone who appreciates your many gifts: the emotional range of a locked freezer, the sexual imagination of a tax form, the moral backbone of a jellyfish in a warm purse. I hope she likes being interrupted by a man who speaks entirely in verdicts. I hope she has strong Wi-Fi, low standards, and a priest on retainer.

As for me, I am done living in the museum of your disappointments, dusting the same exhibits: Your Childhood. Your Ex. Your Big Dream. Your Bad Week. Your Mysterious Inability to Buy Toilet Paper Without Being Praised Like a War Hero.

I am taking my books, my blue mug, the good knife, and the version of myself I buried under your need. If you hear something tonight, something soft dragging itself up from beneath your bed, don’t worry. It’s only the love I had for you, finally dead, looking for a place to rot.

Do not call. Do not text. Do not send one of your long, damp messages pretending accountability is a font choice. If I wanted to be haunted, I’d buy a Victorian with a nursery.

We’re through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a voice-driven monologue from someone who used to worship their beloved but now sees them as rotten and false; use repeated “used to be,” visceral details, nested castle/vault imagery, and the line “your breath stinks.”
counterfactuals.output:
I used to be on my knees for you.

I used to be a hymn with your name caught in my teeth. I used to be the little fool polishing the altar, lighting the candles, sweeping up the ash after you passed through a room like weather. I used to be grateful for any scrap of you—your hand on my shoulder, your laugh in the doorway, the way you looked at me when you wanted to be believed.

I used to be blind enough to call that love.

But now I see the flies.

Now I see the sweetness was spoiled from the start, sugared meat left out too long in a warm room. Now I see the gold leaf peeling off your face, the saint-mask sweating, the halo nailed crooked to a skull full of maggots. I can smell what you are beneath the perfume. I can see the wet rot behind your smile.

Your breath stinks.

And not just of wine, not just of sleep, not just of old secrets fermenting behind your tongue. It stinks of every promise you chewed up and spat into my hands. It stinks of every “trust me” that came out slick and gray. It stinks of the cellar you kept inside yourself, that private underground where you stored the truth in barrels and let it sour.

I used to be the guard at your castle gate.

I used to be the banner snapping above your highest tower. I used to be the bridge lowered for you, the stones warmed by your returning feet. I used to be the fool who thought the castle was sacred because you lived in it.

But your castle had another castle inside it. And inside that, a locked keep. And inside the keep, a vault. And inside the vault, a smaller vault, black iron, sweating cold. And inside that, there you were—not a treasure, not a king, not my beloved, but a little rotten thing curled around its own lies, guarding a crown made of teeth.

I used to be afraid to open the doors.

I used to be afraid of what I’d find if I followed the smell down the stairs, past the tapestries, past the prayer room, past the portraits where you had painted yourself beautiful. I used to be afraid the truth would ruin me.

But it ruined you instead.

Look at you. The velvet is mold. The goblet is rust. The throne has worms in the joints. Your roses are black at the stem. Your mouth is a wound pretending to sing.

I used to be yours.

I used to be.

Now I am the torch in the corridor. Now I am the key turned hard in the lock. Now I am the echo that won’t kneel. Now I am standing in the deepest chamber of you, holding up the light, watching all your hidden things twitch and pale.

And I do not worship rot.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
